article_blocks.text: Strain Type: Balanced hybrid
Genetics: Punjab, North India landrace-derived genetics
Breeder: Mandala Seeds
THC Content: 24%
CBD Content: Not officially specified
Terpene Profile: myrcene , limonene , caryophyllene
Primary Flavors: Sweet fruit, apricot, citrus, herbs, mild earth
Flowering Time (Indoor): 65 days
Outdoor Harvest Time: Late September
Indoor Yield: 400–500 g/m²
Outdoor Yield: 850–1,000 g per plant
Grow Difficulty: Easy; well suited to beginners

White Satin comes from an earlier period of cannabis breeding when Mandala Seeds deliberately looked beyond the established Dutch gene pool for fresh landrace material. Rather than being another member of the White Widow family, despite what the name might suggest, this cultivar was developed from genetics originating in Punjab, northern India. Mandala selected the line for uncomplicated cultivation, strong flower production, low odor while growing, and an unusually social high that remains mentally engaging instead of becoming immediately sedative.

The breeder ultimately discontinued White Satin, but its reputation has survived because it combined several qualities rarely found together: a medium-sized structure, approximately 65 days of flowering, substantial yields, dense resinous colas, and a sweet fruit aroma touched by apricot. Mandala’s archived breeder listing identifies the strain simply as an indica-sativa hybrid with Punjab genetics and gives indoor production of 400–500 g/m² along with outdoor yields reaching 850–1,000 grams per plant.
Genetics and Lineage

Mandala Seeds identified White Satin’s foundation as landrace genetics from Punjab in northern India rather than giving a familiar commercial two-parent formula. That distinction is important because several newer cultivars carrying the White Satin name have been assigned completely different pedigrees. The original Mandala strain is not Gorilla Glue × Blue Dream , nor is it White Widow crossed with a Haze variety. Its documented identity is an indica-sativa hybrid built from Indian genetic material selected within Mandala’s breeding program.

Punjab sits at an important geographic crossroads in traditional cannabis history. Cannabis populations from northern India can display a wide range of traits, from compact, resin-oriented plants associated with hash production to taller, more cerebral expressions. White Satin reflects that diversity unusually well. Some plants lean toward compact indica-style growth and dense flowers, while others grow somewhat taller and express a clearer, more uplifting high. Historical grow observations documented both indica-leaning and more sativa-oriented phenotypes within the population, generally finishing within only a few days of one another.

Mandala intentionally maintained that balanced character instead of forcing the cultivar toward one extreme. The result grows with enough indica influence to remain manageable indoors, yet its effects and social character reveal a substantial sativa side. That genetic balance is one of the reasons White Satin became popular with growers looking for something different from the increasingly standardized Dutch hybrids of its era.
Effects and Experience

White Satin is most memorable for producing a high that remains active and sociable. Mandala described the effect as stimulating, strong but pleasant, uplifting, and particularly suitable for recreational situations because it leaves room for conversation and other activities. The breeder even characterized it as a type of “party” cannabis associated with sociability and laughter. Rather than beginning with a heavy body stone, moderate amounts tend to brighten mood and increase interest in surroundings.

The cerebral quality is noticeable without necessarily becoming sharp or nervous. Music, movies, casual socializing, walks, and creative hobbies can fit the experience particularly well. Historical growers also described a clear-headed state in which sensory impressions such as sound and visual detail became more interesting while the body remained relaxed. This places White Satin somewhere between a functional daytime strain and a more immersive recreational hybrid.

Physical relaxation gradually appears later, especially in plants leaning toward the indica phenotype. Muscles may loosen and the pace slows, but the strain is not generally remembered as a powerful couch-lock cultivar. Larger doses can naturally produce stronger intoxication and reduced concentration. Because Mandala did not publish a fixed THC percentage and the original seed line is now discontinued, modern flowers carrying the name should be judged by batch-specific testing rather than an assumed potency figure.
Medical Benefits

The uplifting yet physically comfortable character historically made White Satin appealing to some medical marijuana consumers. Mandala’s original material mentioned depression, anxiety, and low motivation among possible areas of interest, reflecting the breeder’s observation that the strain could produce a cheerful and active mental state. Consumers seeking cannabis that does not immediately cause lethargy may find this type of effect more practical during the day or early evening.

The calmer second half of the experience may also appeal to people dealing with temporary physical tension or difficulty unwinding. However, breeder-era medical descriptions should not be interpreted as clinical evidence. White Satin itself has not been established through controlled trials as a treatment for depression, anxiety, pain, or any other medical disorder. Cannabis can affect individuals very differently, and stimulating THC-rich weed may actually increase anxiety or rapid heartbeat in sensitive users.

Medical consumers should therefore consider the tested cannabinoid profile of the actual product whenever available. This is especially important with discontinued cultivars, where modern material sold under the same name may not be genetically identical to the original Mandala release.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

White Satin’s aroma is far more delicate during cultivation than its finished flavor might suggest. Mandala specifically noted that flowering plants produce relatively little odor, making the cultivar useful where strong garden fragrance is undesirable. After drying and curing, however, the flowers develop a noticeably sweeter personality. The breeder described the aroma as sweet and fruity with a touch of apricot.

That apricot note is the most distinctive element. Instead of the syrupy berry or candy aromas common in modern marijuana, White Satin tends toward stone fruit, mild citrus, herbs, and soft floral sweetness. Some phenotypes add earthy or slightly creamy undertones, while others emphasize citrus more strongly. Historical growers reported differences between earthy sativa-leaning plants and compact examples with stronger citrus character.

No standardized terpene panel survives from the original breeder stock. Limonene could plausibly contribute citrus brightness, myrcene may support fruit and earth, and caryophyllene could provide subtle spice. Those associations remain sensory interpretations rather than confirmed universal chemistry.
Growing Information

Ease of cultivation was one of White Satin’s major selling points. Mandala explicitly recommended it to both novices and experienced growers, describing a robust plant that performs with relatively little effort. Plants stay medium in height and focus much of their flowering energy on a large central cola, although side branches also produce worthwhile buds. This structure makes the cultivar suitable for Sea of Green arrangements, while enough lateral development remains for SCROG cultivation.

White Satin is also unusually tolerant of modest lighting. The breeder noted acceptable performance under fluorescent lighting, CFL systems, and approximately 150–250-watt HID setups, although stronger lighting naturally allows greater production. Indoor flowering takes approximately 65 days, with dry yields listed at 400–500 g/m². Outdoors, Mandala reported approximately 850–1,000 grams per plant when grown directly in the ground under favorable conditions.

One cultivation issue deserves particular attention: the central cola can become extremely large and dense. Mandala recommended keeping humidity around 35–50% and avoiding nighttime temperatures below roughly 20°C during sensitive stages to reduce mold risk. Large head buds should be inspected internally before harvest when humidity has been high. Outdoors, most plants finish around the end of September in southern regions, while very northern climates may push harvest into mid-October or later.

Nutrient requirements are relatively modest. Historical growers repeatedly described White Satin as undemanding and capable of performing well without heavy feeding. That combination of moderate size, forgiving nutrition, low growing odor, and substantial yield helps explain why the cultivar developed a reputation as an excellent beginner strain.
FAQ
What are the genetics of White Satin?

The original White Satin from Mandala Seeds was developed from landrace-derived cannabis genetics originating in Punjab, northern India. Mandala did not publish a conventional two-parent strain formula.
Is White Satin indica or sativa?

Mandala classified White Satin as an indica-sativa hybrid rather than assigning a strict percentage. Plants can display both compact indica-oriented and somewhat taller sativa-oriented expressions, while the high generally remains uplifting and clear rather than heavily sedating.
What does White Satin taste like?

Sweet fruit and apricot are the signature flavors, supported by citrus, mild earth, herbs, and occasional floral or creamy notes. Mandala specifically described the aroma as sweet-fruity with an apricot accent.
How long does White Satin take to flower?
Indoor flowering takes approximately 65 days. Outdoor plants generally finish near the end of September in southern climates and around mid-October or later in colder northern regions.
Is White Satin still available from Mandala Seeds?

The original White Satin has been discontinued and is listed by Mandala Seeds as sold out and no longer produced. Preserved seeds, clones, or modern cultivars carrying the same name may still circulate, but provenance is important when trying to locate the authentic Mandala line.
Final Thoughts on White Satin

White Satin stands out because Mandala Seeds built it around fresh Indian genetics rather than another remix of famous Dutch cannabis strains . Punjab-derived ancestry gave the breeder enough variation to produce a marijuana cultivar with compact flowering behavior, strong resin production, and an energetic social high within the same population. Its sweet apricot character adds another point of distinction, especially compared with the Skunk, fuel, and candy profiles that dominate many modern hybrids.

From a grower’s perspective, the strain was remarkably practical. Approximately 65 days of flowering, 400–500 g/m² indoor yield, potentially enormous outdoor plants, low odor during bloom, modest feeding requirements, and good performance under relatively weak lighting made White Satin accessible even to newer cultivators. The only major caution is the exceptionally dense central cola, which demands humidity control as harvest approaches.

Although Mandala Seeds eventually retired the cultivar, White Satin remains an interesting piece of cannabis breeding history. It represents a period when breeders were actively introducing less-commercialized regional genetics into modern seed lines, and its combination of Punjab ancestry, apricot sweetness, clear social effects, and straightforward cultivation gave it an identity that remains distinct from the many unrelated strains later marketed under similar names.
